A1.justification: Both nine-page PDFs provide readable text, equations, figures and tables for the same gaze-uncertainty calibration work, despite substantial revisions. Neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: V2 reports original calibration experiments on MPIIGaze and RTGene, including prediction ranges, coverage errors and comparisons with uncalibrated models in Tables I–IV.

after.justification: V4 reports original CPE, error–uncertainty correlation, angular-error and interval-coverage results in Tables 1–2, together with calibration-sample sensitivity experiments.

M1.justification: The ResNet-18/50 architecture, heteroskedastic loss and isotonic calibration remain. V4 extends the reported inference procedure to calibrated median gaze-angle predictions for angular-error evaluation; v2 focuses calibration on uncertainty intervals. The new quantile pseudocode has a mapping inconsistency, rather than clearly establishing a different underlying calibration implementation.

E1.justification: Both retain MPIIGaze and RTGene. However, v2 separately evaluates calibration and testing on the same versus different people under within- and cross-dataset training. V4 retains subject-specific calibration/testing and defines four settings through dataset combinations, removing the separate calibration-to-new-person transfer scenarios.

E2.justification: The evaluated baseline methods remain uncalibrated heteroskedastic regression and pinball/quantile regression. V4 retains both in the corresponding 95% interval comparison, Table 2. Its new distribution-based CPE comparison excludes quantile regression because it lacks a full predictive distribution; newly cited methods are not additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: V2 primarily evaluates joint 95% interval coverage using RMSE and prediction width, with 100 samples for same-person calibration. V4 uses 50 calibration samples for summary results, introduces probability-grid CPE, EUC and angular-error evaluation, and reports direct interval coverage. Both retain three-fold cross-validation and both ResNet sizes.

E4.justification: V4 adds calibration-sample sensitivity at 10, 20, 50 and 100 samples, plus CPE-versus-EUC curves and an error–uncertainty scatter analysis. V2's explicit comparison of successful versus mismatched calibration/test distributions is reduced to the successful case. The 95% interval case study continues an existing evaluation rather than introducing a new task.

E5.justification: V4 adds Mann–Whitney U testing: Table 1 marks CPE differences at p < 0.05 and states p-values of 1 for EUC and angular errors. V2 reports descriptive error distributions without significance tests. Neither introduces seed-based repeated-run reporting; three-fold cross-validation already appears in v2.

E6.justification: V4 replaces v2's prediction-width/RMSE tables with CPE, EUC, angular-error and coverage results. Newly reported calibrated CPE values are 4.63–5.26%, versus 17.50–27.21% uncalibrated. Angular error generally decreases, but RTGene-to-MPIIGaze ResNet-50 increases from 13.76 to 14.24 degrees. These are results under revised protocols, not demonstrated same-setting gains over v2.

T1.justification: V4 introduces a formal probability-grid CPE definition and characterizes it as a proper scoring measure, extending v2's interval-specific coverage formulation. It removes the runtime-complexity subsection. Its new Equation 4 and Algorithm 2 use F^-1(R(p)), which conflicts with the retained definition of the calibrated CDF as R composed with F.

C1.justification: V4 elevates CPE and its claimed superiority to EUC into a central contribution, adds an angular-accuracy benefit, and frames calibration as conditional-distribution matching. V2 instead emphasizes how calibration/test similarity governs reliability and how training-domain variation has limited influence. The claimed contribution therefore changes substantially beyond additional supporting experiments.

C2.justification: V4 adds a median-based explanation for angular improvements and a population-level interpretation of uncertainty scoring. Although it retains the assumption that calibration data represent testing data, it drops v2's substantial discussion of mismatch causing excessive intervals, underconfidence and rejection of good predictions, reducing the treatment of demonstrated failure conditions.

D1.justification: V4 adds CPE/calibration pseudocode and a code/project link. However, it removes v2's PyTorch disclosure, normalization reference, learning rate of 0.0001, learning-rate schedule, batch size of 64 and 50-epoch training budget. This substantially changes reproducibility documentation without establishing that those underlying training settings changed.

R1.justification: V4 substantially repositions the work around distribution matching and uncertainty evaluation, adding Brier, proper-scoring-rule literature and recent gaze-uncertainty research. It removes Kuleshov et al., which v2 explicitly credits as the source adapted for calibration. These changes affect methodological attribution and contribution positioning, not merely bibliography formatting.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work and discussion are extensively rewritten. Separate calibration-goal and evaluation sections are replaced by a metric-first methodology; the network description moves into experiments, and scenario-organized results become accuracy and metric-comparison sections followed by a case study. Author information also changes.

P2.justification: V4 redraws the overview figure, revises reliability displays, adds dataset examples, sensitivity plots, correlation analysis and algorithm boxes, and reorganizes four scenario tables into two evaluation tables. The architecture diagram is retained and relocated. These are substantial changes to visual explanation and layout, beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: V4 adds useful distribution-wide evaluation, sample-size sensitivity, angular-error results and significance reporting. However, it removes informative calibration-transfer failures, training details and explicit prior-method attribution. Its new Equation 4 and Algorithm 2 also conflict with the stated calibration mapping, creating a correctness and reproducibility ambiguity. These substantive benefits and harms prevent a reliable net quality judgment from the supplied PDFs.
